name: Synapse Multi-Hop Benchmark v1
description: A hand-written corpus on the history of computing and AI, plus bridge-style multi-hop questions. 18 'core' passages carry every fact the questions need; 16 'distractor' passages are on adjacent topics, so top-k retrieval has to compete for its slots the way it does on a real corpus. Eight of those distractors do mention a required entity in passing (IBM in d04 and d05, Stanford University in d07, Deep Blue in d10, Google in d11, Retrieval-Augmented Generation in d12, GPU in d13, Transformer in d14). That is deliberate and realistic: no distractor is ever NEEDED to answer a question, and a mention a distractor leaks can only help the passage baseline, never GraphRAG — the 'distractors_leaking_required_facts' list below is asserted by a test so the count cannot silently drift. Three design rules make the questions honestly multi-hop: (1) no single passage contains all of a question's required facts; (2) a question may name at most ONE of its required facts — the anchor — and shares no stemmed content word with the NAME or the DESCRIPTION of any other required fact, so the rest cannot be reached by lexical overlap; (3) no entity description names another entity, so relationships live in the graph rather than being smuggled into the text every system reads. The entity/relationship extraction ships pre-computed, so the benchmark is deterministic and needs no LLM; the only model involved is the local fastembed embedder, used identically by every system under test.
author: Ahmed Maaloul <ahmed.maaloul@proton.me>

passages.text: Ada Lovelace, a British mathematician, published the first algorithm ever written for a machine. Her 1843 notes argued that the Analytical Engine could manipulate arbitrary symbols, not merely numbers.

The Analytical Engine was a mechanical general-purpose computer designed by Charles Babbage in 1837. It was never completed in his lifetime, yet its design already contained a mill, a store, and punched cards for input.

Punched cards were borrowed from the Jacquard Loom, a weaving machine steered by holes in stiff cardboard. Herman Hollerith adapted them for the 1890 United States census and founded the Tabulating Machine Company on the proceeds.
The Tabulating Machine Company merged with three rivals in 1911, and the combined firm was renamed IBM in 1924. IBM went on to dominate business computing for most of the twentieth century.
Deep Blue was a chess-playing machine built by IBM. In 1997 it beat the reigning world champion Garry Kasparov over six games, a result widely read as a milestone for Artificial Intelligence.

Alan Turing formalised computation in 1936 with the Turing Machine, an abstract device that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape. During the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park, where he helped break the Enigma cipher.
In 1950 Alan Turing proposed the imitation game, known today as the Turing Test, as an operational replacement for the question of whether machines can think.

The Dartmouth Workshop of 1956 gave the field of Artificial Intelligence its name, six years after Alan Turing had published his imitation game. It was organised by John McCarthy, who also created the Lisp programming language.

Frank Rosenblatt built the Perceptron, an early trainable classifier wired up in hardware at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. A 1969 book by Marvin Minsky dwelt on what it could not learn, and the disillusionment that followed became the first AI Winter.

Backpropagation, popularised by Geoffrey Hinton and his co-authors in 1986, made it practical to train the multi-layer networks whose absence had doomed the Perceptron. Cheap gradients pulled the field out of its first slump.

AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet competition by a margin no hand-engineered system could match. It was trained on a pair of consumer GPU cards by Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever, supervised by Geoffrey Hinton.
ImageNet is a labelled image database assembled under the direction of Fei-Fei Li at Stanford University. Its annual contest became the yardstick by which progress in Computer Vision was measured.

The Transformer architecture was introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, written by researchers at Google. It threw out recurrence in favour of Self-Attention, letting every token attend to every other token in parallel.
BERT and GPT are both stacks of Transformer blocks. BERT was released by Google and reads a sentence in both directions at once, while GPT predicts the next token strictly left to right.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a research laboratory, with Ilya Sutskever as its first chief scientist. It went on to release the GPT family of models.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds a Large Language Model in passages fetched at query time. It cuts hallucination, but each passage is ranked on its own, so facts that only make sense together are often retrieved apart.

GraphRAG first extracts a Knowledge Graph from the corpus, then walks its edges instead of ranking isolated passages. That traversal is what lets it answer questions Retrieval-Augmented Generation cannot.
Neo4j is a graph database queried with Cypher. Synapse keeps its Knowledge Graph in Neo4j and expands outward from seed entities to assemble reasoning paths.

ENIAC was unveiled in 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania as the first general-purpose electronic computer. Programming it meant rewiring plugboards by hand, and its builders pointed at the Turing Machine as the model of what such a device could in principle compute.
Colossus was a family of code-breaking machines put into service at Bletchley Park in 1944. Built from thermionic valves, they attacked the Lorenz teleprinter traffic rather than the naval ciphers.

The stored-program idea was set out in a 1945 report on EDVAC written by John von Neumann. Keeping instructions in the same memory as the data became the standard layout for every machine that followed ENIAC.
The Transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947 and swiftly displaced the fragile valve. IBM shipped its first fully transistorised computer just over a decade later.
Fortran, released by IBM in 1957, was the first widely used high-level programming language. It let scientists write formulas instead of raw machine instructions.
Grace Hopper championed English-like programming and drove the design of Cobol at the end of the 1950s. Cobol arrived two years after Fortran and was aimed squarely at business data processing.
ARPANET carried its first packets in 1969 between four American research sites, one of them Stanford University. Packet switching rather than dedicated circuits is what made the network resilient.
Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first browser and the first server at CERN in 1990, creating the World Wide Web. It rode on the packet protocols that ARPANET had established two decades earlier.

Expert Systems encoded human rules of thumb as long if-then chains, and MYCIN diagnosed blood infections that way in the 1970s. Their brittleness outside the encoded rules disappointed buyers and deepened the second AI Winter.

Claude Shannon sketched how a machine might play chess in a 1950 paper, decades before any hardware could do it, and his sketch anticipated systems like Deep Blue. He had already founded Information Theory two years earlier.
AlphaGo beat a professional Go player in 2016 using Reinforcement Learning and millions of self-played games. It was built by DeepMind, which Google had acquired two years earlier.
Word2Vec showed in 2013 that words could be placed in a space where distance means similarity. Vector Search over such Embeddings is what Retrieval-Augmented Generation ranks passages with.
NVIDIA released CUDA in 2007, letting ordinary code run on graphics hardware. Cheap parallel arithmetic on a GPU is what made deep networks affordable to train at all.
LSTM networks handled sequences by carrying a gated memory across time steps. They dominated machine translation until the Transformer made recurrence unnecessary.
Fine-Tuning adapts a pretrained network to a narrow task with a small labelled set. It competes with prompting as a way to steer a Large Language Model.
A Vector Database such as FAISS indexes Embeddings so that nearest-neighbour lookup stays fast at scale. It is the storage layer most retrieval pipelines reach for first.
